Memory, Place & the Human Mind

An independent inquiry into how people experience Holocaust memorial sites—and how memory connects history, emotion, and learning.

I’m Alejandra Martínez Beltrán, a high school student at Choate Rosemary Hall. I began this research on my own, outside a school assignment, because I wanted to explore a question that crosses the boundaries between neuroscience and history: how do we remember experiences we did not live through?

“How could the same brain capable of creating such wonderful ideas be vulnerable enough to lose them?”

A question from my personal writing that helped shape my interest in memory and neuroscience
The research question

Where history meets human experience

My curiosity about the brain began with memory and identity. I wanted to look at that question from another direction: how do communities preserve memories of experiences that later generations did not witness?

During summer 2026, I pursued this question independently at Holocaust sites of memory in Poland, France, and the Czech Republic. My study examined visitors’ and staff members’ perceptions of remembrance, emotions, resilience, symbolic reparation, and the transmission of history. I interpreted these qualitative findings alongside research on emotion and episodic memory.

NeuroscienceHistorical memoryEmotionEducationHuman dignity
Research in the field

Three countries, many ways of remembering

During summer 2026, I observed 12 sites across Poland, France, and the Czech Republic and conducted 24 anonymous interviews at nine of them, using an exploratory qualitative approach.

Insights from qualitative research

What the interviews suggested

These are exploratory interpretations of a small qualitative sample, not claims of universal visitor experience or demonstrated neurological effects.

01 / EDUCATION

Remembering is an active responsibility

Participants frequently emphasized preserving history, acknowledging victims, and reflecting on how to prevent future violence.

02 / EMOTION

There is no single emotional response

Visitors reported sadness, shock, empathy, disbelief, admiration, hope, and sometimes less intense reactions.

03 / PLACE

Physical spaces can make history tangible

Some participants described the experience of being present at a historical site as especially vivid and meaningful.

04 / MEMORY

Personal meaning meets collective history

Objects, images, names, and testimony may connect public remembrance to individual experiences and associations.

Research limitation: the study included 24 interviews, with different questions asked at some sites. It did not measure neural activity, cognition, therapeutic effects, or long-term learning outcomes.

Looking forward

Science with a human purpose

My interest in neuroscience began with questions about how memory shapes identity, and how it can change or disappear. This independent project let me investigate a different dimension of memory: the meanings people attach to historical places and to the stories preserved there.

I plan to continue exploring this subject through my Capstone at Choate Rosemary Hall. That future school project will build on—not replace or retroactively define—the independent fieldwork I began in summer 2026.

About my submitted research

Manuscript abstract

Research manuscript · 5 pages · Not peer-reviewed or published

The preservation of Holocaust memory raises questions about how societies transmit historical experiences to generations that did not live through them directly and how these acquire meaning in individual and collective memory.

This exploratory study integrates historical memory studies with neuroscience literature. It draws on direct observations of twelve sites and 24 anonymous interviews conducted at nine sites in Poland, France, and the Czech Republic.

Participants described memorial sites as places of remembrance and historical learning, while expressing varied emotional responses and differing views about symbolic reparation. The study does not establish causal, therapeutic, or neurobiological effects.

Editorial note: This is a reader-friendly abridgment of the original abstract, not a published journal abstract or a claim of acceptance.

The complete manuscript is not available on this website while it is under editorial consideration. This page presents selected information from the independent research.
